6250:
Flamboyance is the quality of being strikingly showy, bold, extravagant, and attention-commanding — in the way someone looks, behaves, speaks, or presents themselves to the world.

When someone has flamboyance, they don't just walk into a room — they make an entrance. They don't simply dress well — they dress to dazzle. Their personality, style, or manner is so vivid and larger-than-life that it's almost impossible to ignore them.

Think of a performer who wears a sequined cape and plays a grand piano on a stage full of candelabras. Or a person who arrives at a party in the most dramatic, colorful outfit in the room and greets everyone with sweeping gestures and theatrical enthusiasm. That quality — that over-the-top, eye-catching boldness — is flamboyance.

Flamboyance can show up in many forms:

In appearance: Wearing extremely bright, clashing, or ornate clothing. Choosing bold accessories, dramatic hairstyles, or unusual combinations that are deliberately designed to stand out.

In behavior and personality: Being theatrical, expressive, and loud in a way that performs for an audience. Big gestures, dramatic reactions, a flair for storytelling, and a tendency to turn everyday moments into a kind of show.

In speech: Using vivid, exaggerated language. Describing things in the most colorful way possible. Never saying "I liked it" when "I was absolutely transfixed by it" will do.

In art, design, or décor: A room filled with gold furniture, rich jewel-toned walls, chandeliers, and bold patterns has flamboyance. A painting with wild, clashing colors and dramatic brushstrokes has it too.

A crucial part of flamboyance is that it is unashamed and intentional. A person with flamboyance isn't accidentally over-the-top — they choose to be that way with full confidence. They are not embarrassed by their boldness; in fact, they embrace it. This is what separates flamboyance from simply being messy or chaotic. There is always a kind of proud, deliberate theatricality to it.
The Tone of the Word: Is It a Compliment or a Criticism?

This is an important nuance. Flamboyance is generally neutral, but leans slightly positive. It is most often used in an admiring or at least affectionate way — to describe someone whose boldness is entertaining, memorable, and energetic.

However, the word can carry a mild undercurrent of excess. If someone says "his flamboyance was a bit much," they are gently suggesting that the person overdid it — that the showiness crossed into self-indulgence. But even then, the word doesn't carry real harshness. It's not an insult. Think of it as sitting somewhere between admiration and gentle amusement.

The feeling the word creates: This person or thing is dazzling, vivid, theatrical — maybe even a little extra — but hard not to watch.

It helps to separate flamboyance from words it might be confused with:

  • Arrogance is about believing you are better than others. Flamboyance has nothing to do with that — a flamboyant person may be completely warm and generous.
  • Loudness (just noise or volume) is not flamboyance. A person wearing a jaw-dropping outfit without saying a word can have tremendous flamboyance.
  • Confidence alone is not flamboyance. A confident person can be understated. Flamboyance is specifically about visible, outward, theatrical display — it must be seen or felt by others.
  • Eccentricity is about being unusual or quirky, often without caring about others' reactions. Flamboyance, by contrast, is almost always aware of its audience. It's a performance.

The word is flexible. You can talk about:

  • A person's flamboyance — their personality, style, way of carrying themselves
  • The flamboyance of a performance — a concert, a speech, a theatrical act
  • The flamboyance of a design, outfit, or piece of art — its visual drama and boldness
  • The flamboyance of someone's speech or writing — its colorful, exaggerated style

Flamboyance exists on a spectrum. A person might have a touch of flamboyance — perhaps they just have a way of telling stories with a bit more drama than most. Or someone might have extraordinary flamboyance — like the rock musician Freddie Mercury, whose stage performances were so theatrical and bold that "flamboyance" barely seems to cover it.

You can signal the degree:

  • "a hint of flamboyance" — subtle but noticeable
  • "unmistakable flamboyance" — clearly and strongly present
  • "extraordinary flamboyance" — at the outermost extreme

• "The fashion designer was known for her flamboyance — every collection was more dramatic and colorful than the last."
  • "There was a certain flamboyance to his speaking style that made even ordinary announcements feel like grand declarations."
  • "The hotel lobby was decorated with a flamboyance that some guests loved and others found overwhelming."
  • "His flamboyance on stage — the costumes, the theatrics, the energy — made him one of the most unforgettable performers of his generation."

"A flamboyance" is also the official collective noun for a group of flamingos — the birds. So you'd say "a flamboyance of flamingos." This is not a coincidence. Flamingos are bright pink, dramatic-looking, and gregarious, making the word a perfect fit. If you ever come across this usage, now you'll know exactly why it was chosen.
Flamboyance is the quality of being boldly, theatrically, and unapologetically showy in appearance, behavior, or style — in a way that commands attention and is impossible to overlook.
6251:
If you remember only one thing about this word, remember this: flamboyant means boldly and dramatically showy — in appearance, behavior, or personality — in a way that is impossible to ignore.

It always carries the sense of something going far beyond the ordinary, the subtle, or the quiet. A flamboyant person, style, or gesture does not whisper. It announces itself loudly and confidently to the whole room.
When Used to Describe a Person

This is the most common use of the word. A flamboyant person is someone who is:

  • Extremely expressive and theatrical in how they speak, move, and behave
  • Very attention-drawing in how they dress or present themselves
  • Confident to the point of being dramatic — they love being seen and noticed
  • Lively, vibrant, and never dull or understated

Think of a performer who sweeps onto a stage wearing an enormous sequined costume, greets the audience with a dramatic gesture, and speaks in grand, sweeping statements. That person is flamboyant. They are not shy. They are not plain. Everything about them is turned up to maximum volume.

A flamboyant person doesn't just walk into a room — they make an entrance.

The word also describes objects, styles, and designs — anything that is visually bold, extravagant, and ornate.

A flamboyant outfit is one with vivid colors, unusual patterns, flashy accessories, and an overall look that says "look at me." A flamboyant gesture is a dramatic, exaggerated physical movement — like throwing your arms wide open when you could simply have nodded. Flamboyant architecture is a building covered in elaborate decorative details, where plain and simple was clearly not an option.

The common thread in all these cases: excess, richness, and deliberate visual impact.

"Flamboyant" is not a mild or moderate word. It sits at the far end of the scale from plain and simple. Something can be slightly colorful, or quite stylish, or fairly bold — but when something is flamboyant, it has gone all the way. It is unmissable. There is nothing accidental or quiet about it.
The Tone: Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

This is an important nuance. The word can be used in all three ways, depending on context and the speaker's attitude.

Used admiringly: "Her flamboyant style is so captivating — she's one of a kind." Here, the speaker finds the quality exciting, creative, and magnetic.

Used neutrally: "He arrived in a flamboyant purple suit." This is simply a factual observation with no clear judgment attached.

Used critically: "The CEO's flamboyant spending habits alarmed the board." Here, "flamboyant" suggests excess that has gone too far — wasteful, irresponsible, over-the-top in a bad way.

So pay close attention to the surrounding words and the speaker's attitude. The word itself is not inherently a compliment or an insult — it depends entirely on who is using it and why.

These words are close in meaning, but each has its own shade:

Showy — similar, but slightly more negative. It almost always implies that someone is trying too hard to impress.

Flamboyant — can be admired; it suggests natural theatrical energy, not just trying to show off.

Ostentatious — more negative than flamboyant. It implies deliberate, excessive display specifically to impress or signal wealth and status.

Flashy — usually negative or informal. A flashy watch or car feels cheap or tacky in its showiness.

Theatrical — refers specifically to dramatic, performance-like behavior. A flamboyant person is often theatrical, but theatrical doesn't always mean flamboyant.

Extravagant — focuses more on spending or excess in amount and scale. A flamboyant person might be extravagant, but you can be extravagant in a quiet, non-flamboyant way (e.g. buying a very expensive but plain car).

Vivid / Colorful — these focus only on visual brightness, while flamboyant captures the whole personality and energy, not just the look.

To truly understand a word, it helps to know its opposite. Flamboyant is the opposite of:

Understated — deliberately quiet and restrained in style.
Modest — avoiding drawing attention to oneself.
Reserved — quiet, self-contained, not expressive.
Plain / Simple — no decoration, no excess, no drama.
Subtle — refined and gentle, easy to miss.

"The singer was known for her flamboyant stage costumes — feathers, sequins, six-inch heels, and all."

"He had a flamboyant personality; even ordering coffee felt like a performance."

"The ballroom was decorated in a flamboyant style, with gold chandeliers and crimson velvet everywhere."

"Critics described the director's debut film as flamboyant but hollow — all style, no substance."

"She dressed conservatively at work, but her weekends were spent in the most flamboyant outfits imaginable."
One Thing to Watch Out For

Because "flamboyant" is such a visually loaded and theatrical word, it is often associated with people in the arts, fashion, or performance. However, the word can describe anyone or anything — a business executive, a sports coach, a piece of furniture, or even a way of speaking. Do not limit it in your mind to only one type of person or setting.
Flamboyant means boldly, dramatically, and theatrically showy — whether in personality, behavior, or appearance — in a way that is impossible to ignore and far beyond what is ordinary or restrained.
6252:
A flame is the hot, glowing, flickering stream of burning gas that you see when something is on fire.

When a substance burns, it releases energy in the form of light and heat. That visible, luminous part — the thing you actually see dancing above a candle, a matchstick, or a campfire — is the flame. It is not the smoke, not the ash, not the burning object itself. It is specifically that bright, wavering ribbon of glowing gas.

"She lit the candle and watched the flame flicker in the breeze."

A flame has a few defining qualities worth knowing:

  • It moves — it flickers, dances, and sways. A perfectly still flame is unusual.
  • It produces both light and heat — you can see by it and feel its warmth.
  • It has a characteristic color — usually some combination of blue at the base (where it's hottest) and orange, yellow, or red toward the top.

You can speak of a flame (one single stream of fire) or flames (many at once, as in a large fire).

"The house was engulfed in flames."
"A single flame burned in the darkness."

Because of the vivid orange-red color of fire, flame is also used as a colour name — a bright, burning orange-red. You might see this in descriptions of hair, fabric, or paint.

"She had flame-red hair that turned heads wherever she went."
"The sunset painted the sky in shades of flame and gold."

Humans have always associated fire with intense feeling — fire burns, consumes, and cannot be easily stopped. So flame came to represent any strong, intense emotion, particularly:

1. Passion or desire

When someone feels an overwhelming romantic or emotional pull toward another person, that feeling is often described as a flame — something burning inside them.

"The flame of his love for her never died."
"She felt the old flame of jealousy reignite."

Notice: you can say a flame burns, grows, flickers (weakens), dies out, or is rekindled — all drawn from how real fire behaves.

2. Any burning intensity

Beyond romance, a flame can stand for any fierce, passionate drive — ambition, anger, creative inspiration, or devotion to a cause.

"The flame of revolution spread through the city."
"He kept the flame of hope alive through years of hardship."

This is a very common expression worth knowing. An old flame means a person you were once romantically involved with — an ex-lover or ex-partner — especially one you still feel some warmth or nostalgia toward.

"She ran into an old flame at the coffee shop."
"He's never quite gotten over that old flame from college."

The image is of a fire that once burned between two people — even if it has since gone out, a trace of warmth (memory, affection) may still remain.

Because fire is also destructive, flames can represent anger, conflict, or destruction:

"Their argument fanned the flames of resentment."
"His cruel words only added fuel to the flames."

The phrase "to fan the flames" means to make an already tense or angry situation worse.
The phrase "to pour fuel on the flames" means the same — to deliberately worsen a conflict.

In the context of the internet, email, and online forums, a flame is a hostile, aggressive, and insulting message sent to someone online — typically an attack on the person rather than a calm disagreement.

"He posted one controversial opinion and immediately received flames from dozens of strangers."

When two people or groups trade these hostile messages back and forth repeatedly, it becomes a flame war — a prolonged, heated online argument full of personal attacks and hostility.

This usage comes from the idea of fire as something that burns, attacks, and destroys.

ContextWhat "flame" means

A flame is always about heat, intensity, and visibility. Whether you're talking about:

  • the literal flicker of fire on a candle,
  • the burning colour of orange-red,
  • an intense passion or emotion,
  • a person you once loved,
  • or a hostile online attack —

…the word flame always carries the sense of something burning brightly, intensely, and with energy. It may warm, it may illuminate, or it may consume — but it is never mild or indifferent.

These are words and phrases that commonly appear alongside flame:

  • burst into flames — to suddenly catch fire
  • go up in flames — to be destroyed by fire, or (figuratively) to fail catastrophically
  • fan the flames — to make a bad situation worse
  • old flame — a former romantic partner
  • flame of passion / desire / hope — an intense feeling
  • flame up — to suddenly flare or intensify

That covers everything you need — the literal, the figurative, the idiomatic, and the modern usage. The word flame is fundamentally about burning intensity in all its forms.
6253:
To flank something or someone means to be at the side of it, or to move to the side of it. The word is all about the side — not the front, not the back, but the side.

Think of it this way: if you are standing directly in front of a building, you are facing it head-on. But the walls running off to your left and right? Those are the flanks. To flank something is to relate to it from that position.

1. To be positioned at the side(s) of something or someone

This is the most common, everyday use. When something flanks something else, it is simply located at its side — like a frame around a picture, but only on the sides.

  • Two tall oak trees flanked the front gate. → The trees stood on either side of the gate, one to the left, one to the right.
  • The president walked onto the stage, flanked by his advisors. → His advisors were right beside him, one on each side.
  • A small café flanked the bookshop on the left. → The café was right next to the bookshop, on its left side.

Notice: the subject does not have to move. This use simply describes where something is — it is sitting there, at the side.

2. To move around to the side of something (especially to gain advantage)

This is the more active, strategic use of the word. Here, someone or something moves to the side of a target — usually to surprise it, attack it, or get around it — instead of approaching it directly from the front.

  • The soldiers flanked the enemy camp. → Instead of charging straight at the enemy, the soldiers swung around to attack from the sides.
  • The faster players flanked the opposing team's defence. → They ran around to the sides rather than pushing through the middle.

In this sense, flanking is about avoiding a direct confrontation and instead coming at something from an angle. It is the opposite of a head-on approach.

In everyday writing and speech, "flanked by" (passive voice) is extremely common. You will see it constantly. It means: something has things on its sides.

  • The throne was flanked by two stone lions. → A lion on each side of the throne.
  • She stood at the podium, flanked by the national flags. → A flag on her left, a flag on her right.
  • The highway was flanked by endless fields of wheat. → Wheat fields stretched along both sides of the highway.

Whenever you see "X was flanked by Y," simply picture Y standing/sitting/placed on the sides of X. That is all it means.

The verb is flexible. Almost anything can flank something else:

  • People can flank other people. (Bodyguards flanked the celebrity.)
  • Buildings or structures can flank each other. (Two towers flanked the entrance to the castle.)
  • Natural things can flank places. (Cliffs flanked the narrow beach.)
  • Soldiers or teams can flank opponents. (The cavalry flanked the infantry.)
The Key Nuance: One Side or Both?

This is subtle but worth knowing.

  • When one thing flanks something, it is usually on one side only.
    A large pillar flanked the statue on the right.
  • When two things flank something, they are typically on both sides — one on the left, one on the right.
    Two large pillars flanked the statue.
  • When something is flanked by a group (like a crowd or a row of trees), the group tends to line both sides, like a corridor.
    The road was flanked by cheering crowds.

No matter how it is used — whether it describes a static position or a military manoeuvre — the word "flank" always points to the side. If you ever see it and feel unsure, just ask yourself: "Is something happening at the side of something else?" The answer will almost certainly be yes, and that is your meaning.
6254:
A flapper is a word that has one very famous, dominant meaning — and that is the one nearly everyone thinks of first: a young woman of the 1920s who deliberately broke away from the traditional rules of how women were supposed to look, behave, and live.

This single meaning is so culturally powerful and so widely remembered that the word "flapper" has essentially become a symbol of an entire era — the 1920s.

To truly understand this word, you need a little context.

Before the 1920s, women in Western society (especially in the United States and Britain) were expected to follow very strict social rules. They were supposed to dress modestly, cover their bodies, keep their hair long and pinned up, stay home or stay quiet, not drink alcohol, not go out alone, and generally behave in a way that was considered "proper" and "respectable." A woman who stepped outside these rules was judged harshly by society.

Then came the 1920s — a decade that historians often call the Roaring Twenties or the Jazz Age. The First World War had just ended, economies were booming (at least for a while), cities were growing, jazz music was everywhere, and a new generation of young people wanted to live differently. Women, in particular, had recently gained the right to vote in the United States (1920) and were feeling increasingly independent.

Into this world stepped the flapper.

A flapper had a very recognizable, distinctive appearance — deliberately designed to shock and challenge the older generation's ideas about femininity:

  • Short, bobbed hair. This was radical. Women had been expected to keep their hair long for centuries. A flapper cut hers short in a style called a "bob" or sometimes a "shingle." This was considered almost scandalous at the time.
  • Short skirts and dresses. Flapper dresses typically fell to just below the knee — which was considered daringly short for the era. The dresses were often loose, straight, and sleeveless, rejecting the corseted, cinched silhouette that had defined women's fashion for decades.
  • Heavy makeup. Red lipstick, darkened eyes, rouge on the cheeks — flappers wore visible, bold makeup at a time when "nice women" were supposed to look natural.
  • Rolled-down stockings. Rather than wearing proper stockings pulled up, flappers would roll them down to the knee. A small but deliberate act of rebellion.
  • Headbands and jewelry. Often a beaded headband across the forehead, long pearl necklaces, dangling earrings — flashy and expressive.
  • Low heels or T-strap shoes suited for dancing.

The overall look was deliberately modern, youthful, boyish in some ways (flat-chested silhouettes were fashionable), and self-expressive rather than demure.

A flapper's behavior was just as striking as her appearance:

  • She went to jazz clubs and dance halls — and she danced energetically, doing dances like the Charleston, the Black Bottom, and the Foxtrot, which older people found wild and inappropriate.
  • She smoked cigarettes in public. This was considered deeply unladylike, and flappers did it openly, often through a long cigarette holder.
  • She drank alcohol — even though the United States was under Prohibition (1920–1933), meaning alcohol was illegal. Flappers drank in underground illegal bars called speakeasies, which added to their rebellious image.
  • She drove cars — a new symbol of independence and freedom in the 1920s.
  • She dated and socialized freely with men, unchaperoned, on her own terms — something that had been heavily restricted for women before.
  • She had a casual, carefree, irreverent attitude toward society's rules and expectations. She was confident, loud, fun, and unapologetic.
  • She worked — many flappers held jobs, which was another sign of economic independence.

Beyond just a style or a set of behaviors, the flapper represented something much bigger: the idea that women could define their own lives, make their own choices, and occupy public space freely and confidently.

She was a cultural revolutionary, even if she didn't call herself one. She challenged the idea that a woman's worth was tied to her modesty, her silence, or her role as a wife and mother. She claimed the right to have fun, to be seen, to be heard, and to take up space.

Older generations — and many conservative voices at the time — were horrified. Newspapers wrote alarmed articles about flappers. Priests and politicians gave speeches condemning them. Parents were scandalized. But flappers didn't much care.

At the same time, the flapper was very much a product of privilege. The lifestyle required money for nice clothes, nights out, and leisure. Most flappers came from the middle or upper-middle class. Working-class women who wanted to could adopt some elements of the style, but the full flapper life was not equally accessible to everyone. And Black women, who were also part of 1920s jazz culture and could be flappers in their own right, were largely ignored in mainstream (white) depictions of flapperdom, despite being central to the music and culture.

The flapper era essentially ended with the Great Depression (which began in 1929), when the economic collapse made the carefree, pleasure-seeking lifestyle of the 1920s feel impossible and even tone-deaf. The cultural mood shifted, and the flapper faded as a living identity — but not from memory.

Today, you will encounter the word "flapper" almost exclusively in historical contexts — in books, documentaries, museums, period films (like The Great Gatsby), Halloween costumes, and themed parties. It is not used to describe contemporary women.

When someone dresses as a "flapper" for a costume party, they are referencing this very specific 1920s image: the bobbed hair, the beaded drop-waist dress, the long pearl necklace, the cigarette holder.

The word also sometimes appears metaphorically to describe someone — particularly a woman — who is bold, unconventional, and refuses to follow society's rules. But this usage is rare and usually self-consciously literary or nostalgic.

Because you want the full picture: "flapper" has a few other, much less common meanings, mostly in older or technical usage:

  • A young bird that is just learning to fly and flaps its wings awkwardly. This is an older British usage and is rarely heard today.
  • A broad, flat, flexible object used to hit something or make a slapping sound — something that literally "flaps." Again, rare in everyday usage.
  • A hinged flap or valve in a mechanical device. Mostly a technical term.

None of these meanings have anywhere near the cultural weight of the 1920s sense. If you hear or read the word "flapper" in virtually any context today, it almost certainly means the Jazz Age young woman.

A flapper is a young woman of 1920s America (and to some extent Britain and other Western countries) who rejected the traditional, restrictive social rules for women and instead lived boldly — with short hair, fashionable clothes, jazz music, dancing, drinking, and a confident, independent spirit. She was a cultural icon of rebellion and modernity in her time, and the word today instantly evokes the style, energy, and attitude of that specific decade.
6255:
Before going into the individual meanings, it helps to understand the soul of this word — the feeling that runs through all of its uses.

When something flares, it does one of two things (sometimes both at once):

  • It suddenly becomes more intense, bright, or active — like a small flame that suddenly roars up.
  • It spreads outward from a narrow point — like the bottom of a bell-shaped skirt.

These two ideas — sudden intensification and widening outward — are the twin hearts of this word. Keep them in mind as you read each meaning below.
Meaning 1: To Burn or Shine with a Sudden Burst of Bright Light

This is the most literal, original sense of the word.

When a flame or a light flares, it suddenly burns much brighter than before, often briefly and unsteadily.

Examples:

  • The candle flared in the wind before going out.
  • The match flared for a second, then died.
  • The bonfire flared when someone threw dry leaves into it.

The key quality here is suddenness. The light doesn't increase gradually — it jumps. It's vivid, bright, and often short-lived.
Meaning 2: To Suddenly Become More Intense, Active, or Violent

This is the most widely used meaning in everyday language. It describes how emotions, conflicts, tensions, or problems can erupt suddenly — like a fire flaring up.

Think of a tense room where everyone is quiet, and then one sharp word is spoken — and suddenly everyone is arguing. That eruption is a flare.

Examples:

  • Tempers flared during the meeting.
  • Violence flared in the city after the announcement.
  • His anger flared the moment he heard what had happened.
  • Tensions between the two countries flared overnight.

Notice that this meaning almost always involves something that was already present but controlled — and then suddenly breaks free. Anger doesn't appear out of nowhere; it flares, meaning it was simmering and then burst out.
Meaning 3: To Suddenly Get Worse (Medical / Physical Conditions)

When a health condition or injury flares (or more commonly, flares up), it means the symptoms suddenly become more severe after a period of being manageable or quiet.

This is extremely common when people talk about chronic illnesses, skin conditions, pain, or allergies.

Examples:

  • Her arthritis flared up badly in the cold weather.
  • His asthma flared after he walked through the dusty construction site.
  • My back injury tends to flare up when I sit for too long.
  • Her eczema flared after she used that new soap.

The medical use perfectly mirrors the fire imagery — a condition that was under control suddenly "catches fire" again.

When someone's nostrils flare, they open wider — spreading outward. This usually happens automatically when a person is angry, breathing hard after exercise, or feeling strong emotion.

Examples:

  • His nostrils flared with rage as he listened.
  • She was breathing heavily, her nostrils flaring with every breath.
  • The horse's nostrils flared as it galloped.

This use connects to the "spreading outward" core idea — the nostrils physically widen.
Meaning 5: To Spread or Open Outward in Shape

When something flares, it gradually widens from a narrow point — like the shape of a trumpet, a wine glass, or a bell.

This meaning is about shape and form, not fire or emotion.

Examples:

  • The skirt flares at the bottom.
  • The trousers flare from the knee downward.
  • The pipe flares at one end to allow a wider connection.
  • The walls of the tunnel flare outward as you reach the exit.

If you imagine a cone lying on its side — narrow at one end, wide at the other — the shape at the wide end is what flaring looks like.

This is so common and important that it deserves its own section.

Flare up = to suddenly start or become worse, especially after a period of calm.

It's used for emotions, conflicts, illnesses, and fires alike. The "up" adds a sense of abruptness — something jumping from calm to intense very quickly.

Examples:

  • The old argument between them flared up again at dinner.
  • The fire, which we thought was out, flared up in the middle of the night.
  • His temper flares up without much warning.
  • Her skin condition has been flaring up lately.

You'll see flare up far more often than plain flare in everyday writing and speech, so it's worth paying special attention to it.
The Qualities That Run Through Every Meaning

No matter which sense of flare you're dealing with, these qualities are almost always present:

1. Suddenness — things that flare do so quickly, not gradually.

2. Intensity — the state after flaring is stronger, brighter, or more severe than before.

3. Often temporary — what flares usually settles back down. A fire flares and then calms. Anger flares and then cools. A disease flares and then goes back to being managed.

4. Visibility — something that flares draws attention. It becomes hard to ignore.

Here's a useful way to remember the word:

Flare = a sudden, intense burst outward — whether of light, emotion, pain, or shape.

Whether you're reading about a fire, a fight, a medical condition, or the cut of a dress, the word flare always carries that same core energy: something breaking out of its contained state, suddenly and forcefully.
A Few More Sentences to Cement Your Understanding

• The pilot flared his engines to slow the aircraft during landing.
  • Old rivalries flared up when the two teams met again.
  • The disease had been dormant for years but flared without warning.
  • At the bottom, the vase flares into a wide, open bowl.
  • Her eyes flared with an emotion he couldn't quite read — anger, or perhaps hurt.

Each of these sentences shows a different facet of the same word — but in every single one, you can feel that same quality: something breaking outward, suddenly, with force.
6256:
Before diving into meanings, understand the image behind this phrase. Picture a fire. It is burning calmly and steadily. Then, suddenly — whoosh — the flames shoot up higher and burn much more intensely. That sudden, sharp burst of intensity is a flare. The word "up" adds the sense of it rising or increasing rapidly.

This visual image of fire suddenly burning brighter is the heart and soul of "flare up." Every meaning of this phrase — whether about health, emotions, or conflicts — comes from this same core idea: something that was quiet or calm suddenly becomes intense, worse, or more violent.

In its most direct, physical sense, "flare up" means for a fire or flame to suddenly burn more strongly or brightly.

  • The campfire flared up when he threw a piece of dry wood into it.
  • Be careful with that gas stove — the flame can flare up without warning.

This is where the phrase was born. Everything else is built on top of this image.

"Flare up" is used far more often in a figurative (non-literal) sense. It is applied in three major areas of life:

1. Medical Conditions

This is one of the most common uses. When a medical condition — especially a long-term or chronic illness — suddenly gets much worse after a period of being calm or manageable, we say it flares up.

Think of it like this: the illness is the fire. It was burning low. Then something triggered it, and suddenly the flames shot up.

  • Her eczema always flares up in cold, dry weather.
  • He was managing his back pain well, but after moving furniture, it flared up badly.
  • Asthma, arthritis, lupus, and migraines are all conditions that are known to flare up.

Key point: it implies the condition was there before, went quiet or was under control, and then came back suddenly and intensely. It is not used for a completely new illness.

2. Emotions — Especially Anger

When a person suddenly becomes very angry, upset, or emotional — especially in a quick, intense, and somewhat uncontrolled way — we say they flare up.

  • He flared up when she criticized his work.
  • Don't bring up that topic around her — she tends to flare up.
  • I didn't expect him to flare up like that over something so small.

This use suggests the anger was quick, sharp, and perhaps surprising — like a flame suddenly shooting upward. It often implies the person is somewhat hot-tempered or reactive.

3. Conflicts, Violence, and Problems

When a conflict, fight, argument, war, or crisis that was calm or under control suddenly becomes intense again, it flares up.

  • Violence flared up in the region after weeks of tense peace.
  • The argument between the two neighbors flared up again at the community meeting.
  • Tensions between the two countries have flared up following the border incident.

This use is very common in news reports and journalism. It always suggests something that had cooled down or was under the surface, and then suddenly erupted again.

"Flare up" as two words is a phrasal verb (an action). But when you want to talk about the event or instance of something flaring up, you turn it into a noun by hyphenating it: a flare-up.

  • She had a flare-up of her arthritis last week. (noun)
  • There was a flare-up of violence near the border. (noun)
  • His flare-up surprised everyone in the room. (noun — referring to his sudden anger)

Think of it this way:

  • Phrasal verb: My condition flared up. → describing the action
  • Noun: I had a flare-up. → referring to the episode or event

"Flare up" is a phrasal verb, which means it is a verb ("flare") combined with a particle ("up") that together create a specific meaning different from the individual words alone.

It is an intransitive phrasal verb, meaning it does not take a direct object. You cannot say "she flared up the meeting". The subject is always the thing that flares up:

  • ✅ His temper flared up.
  • ✅ The conflict flared up.
  • ✅ Her skin condition flared up.
  • ❌ He flared up the argument. (incorrect)

Tense examples:

  • Present: My knee flares up when I run.
  • Past: The situation flared up overnight.
  • Future: The rash might flare up again if you skip the medication.
  • Present perfect: The conflict has flared up twice this month.

"Flare up" is neutral in tone — it fits comfortably in everyday conversation, medical discussions, news writing, and formal writing alike. It is not slang, not overly formal, and not offensive in any way. You can use it freely in almost any context.
Common Collocations (Words Often Used With "Flare Up")

Certain words appear very naturally alongside "flare up." Knowing them will help you recognize and use the phrase naturally:

  • Tensions flared up.
  • Violence flared up.
  • A condition flares up.
  • Symptoms flare up.
  • Tempers flared up.
  • Old rivalries flared up.
  • The situation flared up.

Notice the pattern: these are usually things that were already present — tensions, conditions, rivalries — and then they suddenly intensified. "Flare up" almost always implies a return or sudden worsening of something pre-existing, not something completely new.
How to Tell the Difference from "Break Out"

Learners sometimes confuse "flare up" with "break out." Here is the key difference:

  • Break out = something begins for the first time, suddenly. (A fire broke out in the warehouse. / War broke out between the nations.)
  • Flare up = something that existed before suddenly intensifies or returns. (Old hostilities flared up again. / Her condition flared up.)

If something is happening for the very first time, use "break out." If it existed before and is suddenly getting worse again, use "flare up."

"Flare up" means to suddenly become more intense, worse, or more violent after a period of calm. Whether it is a fire, a health condition, a person's emotions, or a political conflict — the phrase always carries the same meaning: a sudden and sharp burst of intensity from something that was previously quiet or under control.
6257: A flare-up is a sudden, often unexpected outbreak or worsening of something — usually something bad — that happens quickly after a period of calm or control.

To truly understand "flare-up," picture a small fire that is barely burning, almost dying out — and then suddenly, a gust of wind hits it, and the flames shoot up violently for a moment. That sudden, dramatic burst is the "flare." A flare-up is that moment — when something that was quiet, controlled, or suppressed suddenly becomes intense and active again.

This image is the heart of the word. Carry it with you, and every use of "flare-up" will make perfect sense.
The key idea behind every use

Three things are almost always true about a flare-up:

  1. It is sudden. It doesn't creep up slowly over weeks. It happens fast — sometimes overnight or even within hours.
  2. It is usually temporary. A flare-up rises quickly, peaks, and then typically settles or calms down again. It is not a permanent state.
  3. It implies something that was already there. This is crucial. A flare-up is not something brand new appearing out of nowhere. It is something — an illness, a conflict, a feeling — that already existed (perhaps quietly or under control) and has now broken out again with force. This sense of recurrence is what makes "flare-up" unique.

1. Medical flare-up (the most common use today)

Many illnesses — especially chronic (long-term) ones — don't stay the same all the time. A person with arthritis, asthma, eczema, lupus, Crohn's disease, or multiple sclerosis, for example, may have long periods where they feel okay and the disease is manageable. But then, sometimes triggered by stress, cold weather, certain foods, or no obvious reason at all, the symptoms suddenly get much worse. That sudden worsening is called a flare-up.

"My sister has eczema. Most of the time her skin is fine, but she had a bad flare-up last winter — her skin became red, cracked, and intensely itchy for two weeks before it calmed down."

"The doctor said the patient was in remission, but she suffered a flare-up of her lupus after a period of stress."

The disease didn't go away — it was just quiet. Then it became suddenly active and severe again. That period of sudden, intense activity is the flare-up.

2. A flare-up of fire or flames

In its more literal sense, a flare-up refers to a sudden burst of fire or flames, especially when a fire that seemed to be dying or under control suddenly grows bigger and more dangerous.

"The firefighters had nearly contained the blaze when a sudden flare-up caused by strong winds sent them retreating."

"There was a dangerous flare-up in the kitchen when oil spilled onto the open flame."

3. A flare-up of conflict, violence, or tension

In news, politics, and international affairs, a flare-up describes a sudden outbreak of fighting, violence, or serious tension — especially in a region or relationship that had been relatively stable.

"After months of fragile peace, there was a sharp flare-up of violence along the disputed border."

"Diplomatic talks broke down, leading to a flare-up of tensions between the two countries."

Again, the conflict was never fully resolved — it was simmering beneath the surface — and now it has burst out suddenly.

4. A flare-up of emotions or temper

A flare-up can also describe a sudden outburst of a strong emotion, most often anger. It happens quickly, it's intense, but it usually passes.

"There was a brief flare-up of anger between the two players on the field, but the referee stepped in and they quickly calmed down."

"His remark caused an unexpected flare-up of frustration in the room."

A flare-up is almost always negative. You will never hear someone describe a "flare-up of joy" or a "flare-up of generosity." The word is reserved for things that cause trouble, pain, danger, or discomfort — illness, fire, conflict, anger.

A flare-up implies a pattern. You don't usually call the very first time something happens a "flare-up." The word suggests this has happened before — or that the underlying problem has been lurking. If someone gets arthritis for the very first time, that's not a flare-up. But after that, each time it suddenly gets much worse, that's a flare-up.

A flare-up can be triggered. Often, a flare-up is set off by something — cold weather, stress, a provocative remark, a political event. That thing is called a trigger. Sometimes there's no clear trigger at all, and the flare-up just happens on its own.

Learning which words naturally pair with "flare-up" will help you use it correctly and recognize it in reading.

  • "A sudden flare-up" — emphasizes how fast it came
  • "A brief flare-up" — emphasizes it didn't last long
  • "A severe / bad flare-up" — emphasizes how intense it was
  • "A flare-up of [condition/problem]" — a flare-up of asthma, a flare-up of violence, a flare-up of tension
  • "A flare-up between [people]" — a flare-up between the two rivals
  • "Suffer / experience a flare-up" — common in medical contexts: "She experienced a flare-up of her condition."
  • "Trigger a flare-up" — "Stress can trigger a flare-up."
  • "Cause a flare-up" — "The comment caused a flare-up of anger."
  • "Have a flare-up" — very natural in everyday speech: "He's having a flare-up."

These words may seem similar, but they each mean something slightly different:

Outbreak — An "outbreak" often refers to something starting or spreading for the first time (like a disease outbreak), not necessarily a recurrence. A flare-up is always about something that already existed becoming active again.

Eruption — Much more dramatic and forceful. An eruption suggests something explosive — like a volcano. A flare-up is sudden and intense, but not necessarily explosive.

Recurrence — A "recurrence" simply means something has come back. It's neutral and doesn't tell you whether it came back suddenly or slowly, mildly or severely. A flare-up, by contrast, always implies it came back suddenly and with intensity.

Episode — In medical language, an "episode" is similar to a flare-up but more clinical and neutral. It doesn't carry the vivid image of something shooting up suddenly the way "flare-up" does.

Surge — A "surge" means a strong increase in something, but it can be gradual and doesn't imply the thing was previously calm or in check.
A final summary to lock it in

A flare-up is a sudden and intense outbreak of something — a disease, fire, conflict, or emotion — that was previously quiet, controlled, or suppressed. It rises quickly, it's usually temporary, and it always implies that the underlying problem was already there. The word is almost always used for something negative, and it carries a vivid image: a flame that shoots up suddenly, burns intensely for a moment, and then — hopefully — dies back down.
6258: A flash flood is a sudden, very fast, and powerful rush of water that overwhelms an area in a very short time — typically within a few minutes to around six hours. The word "flash" is key here: it signals speed and surprise. Unlike a regular flood that builds slowly over days, a flash flood strikes almost without warning, the same way a camera flash happens in an instant.

Imagine a dry or calm road, a stream, or a valley. Within minutes, a massive wall or surge of water — carrying mud, rocks, debris, and even large objects like cars or trees — comes crashing through. The water is not calm and gentle. It moves violently and at great speed. It can be loud. It can be brown and murky from the soil and material it has picked up along the way.

The most common cause is intense rainfall in a short period. When rain falls faster than the ground can absorb it, the water has nowhere to go — so it collects rapidly and rushes downhill along any path it can find.

Other causes include:

  • A dam or levee breaking, suddenly releasing a large stored body of water.
  • Rapid snowmelt, where warm temperatures melt snow too quickly for the ground or rivers to handle.
  • A blocked river or channel that suddenly gets cleared, releasing water all at once.

Sometimes the rain doesn't even fall in the exact place that floods. Rain falling far upstream in the hills or mountains can cause a flash flood in a dry valley miles away — with perfectly clear skies above you. This is one reason flash floods are so dangerous: you may not see them coming.

Flash floods can happen almost anywhere, but certain places are especially vulnerable:

  • Canyons and narrow valleys: Water rushing off higher ground has no room to spread, so it concentrates and accelerates.
  • Dry riverbeds and streambeds (called "wadis" in some regions): These look completely dry but can fill in minutes.
  • Urban and city areas: Concrete and asphalt cannot absorb water at all. Rain water flows straight off roads and pavements into drains, underpasses, and low-lying streets, quickly overwhelming the drainage system.
  • Hilly or mountainous regions: Steep slopes cause water to run off fast rather than soak in.
  • Areas after wildfires: Burned land loses its ability to absorb water, making flash flooding far more likely.
Why Flash Floods Are So Dangerous

Flash floods are considered one of the most deadly natural hazards in the world. Here's why:

  1. Speed of onset: You may have almost no warning. In the time it takes to make a decision, the water can already be upon you.
  2. Force of the water: Moving water is incredibly powerful. Just 15 centimetres (6 inches) of fast-moving water can knock a person off their feet. About 60 centimetres (2 feet) of rushing water can sweep away a car.
  3. Debris: The water doesn't come alone. It carries rocks, branches, furniture, vehicles, and anything else in its path, turning them into battering rams.
  4. People underestimate it: Many deaths occur because people try to walk or drive through flooded roads, believing the water is shallow or slow. A road covered in water can be concealing a completely washed-away surface underneath.
  5. Nighttime strikes: Flash floods frequently happen at night when people are asleep and unaware.
How It Differs From a Regular Flood

It helps to compare the two:

A regular flood is gradual. Rivers slowly rise over several hours or days because of prolonged rainfall or seasonal conditions. People usually have time to prepare, evacuate, or move belongings to safety.

A flash flood is sudden and explosive. It's defined by its speed and the short time between the cause (like heavy rain) and the flood itself. There is little to no time to react. The danger is immediate.

Think of it this way: a regular flood is like water slowly filling a bathtub — you can see it happening and respond. A flash flood is like someone suddenly dumping a huge bucket of water over your head — by the time you realise it, you're already drenched.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "A flash flood swept through the canyon, destroying campsites and blocking roads."
  • "Residents were warned to move to higher ground as a flash flood was expected."
  • "The car was found overturned in the ditch after a flash flood struck the village overnight."
  • "Flash floods are common in desert regions during monsoon season."

A flash flood is a rapid, sudden, and powerful surge of water caused by intense rain or other events, arriving with little warning and capable of causing serious destruction and loss of life within minutes. Its defining quality is speed — it "flashes" into existence. It is not a slow rise of water but a sudden, often violent deluge that can strike any low-lying area, dry streambed, or urban street, and it demands immediate action to stay safe.
6259:
A "flash in the pan" is something — a person, a product, a trend, a moment of success — that starts with a big, exciting burst but quickly fizzles out and amounts to nothing lasting.

It's used for things that look incredibly promising at first but fail to deliver real, lasting results.

Think of it this way: imagine a firework that goes up in the sky with a loud bang and a bright flash... and then produces zero colour, zero sparkle, and just disappears into darkness. That disappointment? That's a flash in the pan.
The Origin — Where Did This Come From?

This idiom has a very literal, physical origin. It comes from old flintlock muskets — the guns used by soldiers and hunters in the 1600s and 1700s, long before modern firearms existed.

Here's how those old guns worked:

  • The gun had a small metal dish near the barrel called a "pan."
  • You'd pour a small amount of gunpowder into this pan.
  • When you pulled the trigger, a piece of flint would strike a spark, which would ignite the powder in the pan.
  • That small ignition was supposed to travel through a tiny hole into the main barrel, which would fire the actual bullet.

But here's the problem — sometimes the powder in the pan would ignite with a dramatic, bright flash... but the flame would fail to reach the barrel. The gun would go "flash!" and then... nothing. No bullet. No shot. Just a lot of noise and light, and then total failure.

That failure had a name: a flash in the pan.

So soldiers and hunters used this phrase to describe something that looked like it was going to work brilliantly, but in the end produced no real result. Over time, the phrase left the world of guns entirely and entered everyday language.

There are two key parts to understanding this idiom:

  1. An impressive, exciting beginning — something grabs everyone's attention. People get excited. It seems like big things are coming.
  2. A disappointing, forgettable end — it fails to follow through. The early promise was an illusion. Nothing meaningful or lasting came of it.

Both parts are essential. If something fails quietly and nobody cared, it's not a flash in the pan. If something succeeds brilliantly and keeps succeeding, it's definitely not a flash in the pan. The idiom specifically describes that painful gap between early excitement and eventual disappointment.

Here are some situations where you'd use this phrase:

In music:

"That band's first song went to number one and everyone thought they'd be huge — but they never released a second hit. Total flash in the pan."

In sports:

"He scored 30 goals in his first season and everyone called him the next great striker. But he never repeated that form. It was a flash in the pan."

In business:

"That app got millions of downloads in its first week, but by the third month, hardly anyone was using it. Flash in the pan."

In politics:

"She burst onto the scene, gave incredible speeches, and everyone said she'd be the future of the party. Two years later, nobody talks about her. Flash in the pan."

In everyday life:

"He started jogging every morning with so much energy. Three weeks later, he quit. That fitness kick was just a flash in the pan."
How to Use It in a Sentence

The phrase is almost always used as a noun phrase. Here are the most natural ways to use it:

  • "It was a flash in the pan." (most common — used after the failure is clear)
  • "He turned out to be a flash in the pan." (talking about a person)
  • "I hope this isn't just a flash in the pan." (expressing worry or doubt about something's staying power)
  • "Don't dismiss it yet — it might not be a flash in the pan." (defending something against early scepticism)
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This phrase carries a mildly negative, slightly dismissive tone. When you call something a "flash in the pan," you're suggesting:

  • It was never as good as it seemed.
  • Its early success was based on hype, luck, or novelty rather than real quality.
  • It didn't have the substance to last.

It's not the harshest criticism in the English language, but it is a put-down. It implies the thing being discussed was never truly deserving of the attention it got.

Importantly, you almost never say this in the moment of initial excitement. You say it after the failure has become obvious — looking back, reflecting, or warning others.

However, it can also be used as a warning or a doubt, like:

"Let's not celebrate yet — this could be a flash in the pan."

In that case, the person hasn't failed yet, but you're cautioning against premature excitement.

These phrases share a similar meaning and are useful to know alongside this one:

  • "One-hit wonder" — someone (usually a musician) famous for just one success, never to be heard from again.
  • "Nine-day wonder" — something that causes excitement for a short time and is then completely forgotten.
  • "Here today, gone tomorrow" — something that disappears as quickly as it appeared.
  • "Fly-by-night" — unreliable, short-lived, and not to be trusted to last.

People sometimes use "flash in the pan" to simply mean "something that happened fast." That's incorrect. Speed alone isn't the point. The phrase specifically requires:

✅ Initial excitement or success
✅ Followed by failure or fading away

A thunderstorm that's intense but brief is not a flash in the pan — because a storm isn't supposed to be a long-term success in the first place. A pop star who dominates charts for one summer and disappears forever? That is a flash in the pan.

If you ever need to recall this idiom in an instant:

"A flash in the pan = something that seemed brilliant at first but turned out to be a short-lived disappointment."

Just picture that old musket going flash! — dramatic, loud, exciting — and then firing absolutely nothing. That image will stick with you every time.
